q: Under the default numeric tolerance, does NodePy's rk_method.order() ever silently mis-classify order for large-stage RK methods where the residual on some Butcher-tree condition is on the order of the tolerance? A systematic order()-vs-order('exact') sweep across the entire loadRKM catalog (with an intentional tolerance ladder 1e-4..1e-16) would map the boundary and identify methods where default tol is unsafe.
basis: In this replication all 11 tested methods matched under both modes, but the sibling attempt reported an SSP53 anomaly resolved only by mode='exact'. The paper does not discuss the default tolerance choice or its failure modes.
next_steps: Add a nose/pytest sweep in nodepy tests that runs both modes across the full loadRKM catalog and asserts equality; open a PR proposing an adaptive tolerance based on |b|_inf * ||A||_F.

q: Should stability_function() return a native floating-point poly1d in addition to (or instead of) the current SymPy-wrapped poly1d? Under Python 3.14 the returned object silently makes np.polyval symbolic on numeric input, causing a 400x400 grid evaluation to hang for tens of minutes. Downstream users who don't know the internal representation cannot detect this via type checks (isinstance says numpy.poly1d).
basis: Directly observed: two full replicate.py runs killed after ~4-8 minutes of 97% CPU on the stability grid before the coefficient-cast fix (np.poly1d(np.array(p.coef, dtype=float))). This is a real correctness/performance surprise induced by the exact/float dual-mode design choice.
next_steps: Add stability_function(exact: bool = False) with float default (or return two separate objects). Add a test that np.polyval(p_returned, complex_array) completes in <1s on a 400x400 grid.

q: Why does rt.list_trees(n) go from ~milliseconds at n=7 to tens of seconds at n=8 and effectively unbounded at n>=10? Does the current enumerator re-generate rooted subforests each call rather than memoizing them, and how much of the p>=6 order-condition machinery is bottlenecked by this?
basis: Observed timing wall in this replication: n<=7 ran in <1s per level; n=8 hung an initial run past 4 minutes before it was killed. Order-conditions for order p require rooted trees of order <=p, so this directly limits the range over which Butcher-tree machinery is practical inside NodePy.
next_steps: Profile rt.list_trees to see if canonical-form checks are quadratic in |forest|; introduce a functools.lru_cache-keyed enumerator; benchmark the improvement on the sixth-order embedded-pair search that motivated the paper's Horvath 2019 citation.

q: The absolute_monotonicity_radius solver in NodePy converged to 1, 1, 6 for SSP22/33/104 with ~1e-10 residual from the theoretical integer. Is the underlying bisection/numerical solver guaranteed to find the global radius, or can it get trapped at a locally-maximal but sub-global c-value for constructed pathological RK methods with multiple monotonicity plateaus?
basis: Empirically all published SSP values were recovered to 1e-10, but the JOSS paper doesn't describe the underlying algorithm. For a validation package used to certify new SSP methods (a stated use case), knowing whether the solver can silently underreport c is important.
next_steps: Construct a synthetic RK Butcher tableau with a known two-plateau monotonicity structure; call absolute_monotonicity_radius from below and above; verify convergence to the global maximum. If not guaranteed, document the caveat or upgrade to a global bracketing method.

q: Does NodePy's built-in DETEST implementation reproduce the original Enright-Hull (1972) DETEST configuration exactly (initial conditions, integration span, evaluation tolerances) so that convergence/performance comparisons against solver-benchmark papers from the 1970s-90s remain meaningful, or has parametrization drifted over the years of development?
basis: The paper advertises DETEST as one of the shipped test suites but the docstrings are the primary documentation and the drift risk is real for a package that has evolved for over a decade. This replication tested empirical convergence on a hand-written y'=y cos(t) rather than a DETEST problem to avoid this ambiguity.
next_steps: Cross-check NodePy's ivp.detest problem definitions (rhs, y0, t0, tf, jacobian) against the Enright-Hull table verbatim; publish a diff and, if any drift exists, gate the classical DETEST identifiers behind an explicit legacy=True flag.
